items.q: Design an image memory cache with LRU eviction
items.prompt:
Design a thread-safe in-memory image cache for an Android app: `get(url): Bitmap?` and `put(url, bitmap)` with LRU eviction and a byte-budget cap.

The real interview is about the *Android* details: size by bytes (not count), evict on the right thread, avoid caching giant bitmaps, and be able to explain why `android.util.LruCache` exists and when you'd write your own (pixel-size accounting, keying by URL + size, disk tier).
hints: An LRU cache needs O(1) get and O(1) eviction — `LruCache` already is that, so the design question is what you key on and what you count.
Count bytes: `sizeOf(key, value)` should return the bitmap's `byteCount`, and the budget should derive from `ActivityManager.memoryClass`.
Thread-safety: `LruCache` is internally synchronized for the common ops — say which ops need *your* locks (reads during eviction, trimming on low memory via `onTrimMemory`).

code.caption: Byte-budget LruCache keyed by URL+size

items.complexity: Time O(1) for get/put on `LruCache`. Space bounded by `maxBytes`. The byte-based `sizeOf` and the memoryClass-derived budget are the two Android-specific answers interviewers grade for.
followUps: Why key by `url@size`? (Two screen densities want different bitmaps for the same URL.)
Why not recycle aggressively? (Only when the cache holds sole ownership — shared bitmaps crash.)
Add a disk tier — what changes about eviction and async loading?

items.prompt:
Implement a custom Compose layout — e.g. a simple `Row`-like composable or a `FlowRow` — using `Layout { }`, and explain the measurement contract.

This tests real Compose fluency, not LeetCode. The contract: `Layout` gets `measurables`, each `MeasurePolicy.measure` returns a `Placeable`; you measure children with `Constraints`, and you must honor incoming `constraints.maxWidth/Height` while placing with `placeRelative`. Name the recomposition vs relayout difference.
hints: Use `Layout(content) { measurables, constraints -> ... }`. Measure each child: `measurable.measure(constraints.copy(minWidth = 0, minHeight = 0))`.
Sum widths for a row, take max height. Clamp to `constraints.maxWidth`. Then `layout(width, height) { children.forEach { it.placeRelative(x, 0) } }`.
Mention `placeRelative` (RTL-aware) over `place`, and that width must respect `constraints.maxWidth` or it will throw.

code.caption: Minimal row layout via Layout {}

items.complexity: One measure pass, one layout pass — O(children) per frame. The interview is about correctness: clamping to max constraints, `placeRelative`, and the single-pass invariant.
followUps: What breaks if you ignore `constraints.maxWidth`? (IllegalStateException at runtime.)
When does a custom layout need *two* passes (e.g. FlowRow needs height from wrap)?

items.q: Implement a minimal StateFlow from scratch
items.prompt:
Implement a minimal `StateFlow<T>`-like class: it holds a value, exposes it, and notifies collectors whenever the value changes — without building on `kotlinx.coroutines.flow`.

The point is the *contract*, not the coroutine machinery: a conflated state holder where collectors always get the latest value, updates are atomic, and multiple collectors each get a replay of the current value on subscribe. Use a `MutableStateFlow` in production; build this to prove you understand conflation and atomicity.
hints: Hold `value` in an atomic or under a lock, plus a list of subscribers that each hold the last-emitted value.
On `set`, atomically update the value, then notify each subscriber whose last-emitted differs — that's the conflation: collectors skip intermediate values.
Subscribe: send the current value immediately, then register. Concurrent set during subscribe must not miss an update — coordinate with the same lock.

code.caption: Thread-safe conflated holder

items.complexity: Time O(subscribers) per update, O(1) per read. The `@Volatile` read is lock-free for `value`; writes serialize under `lock`. Compare with real `StateFlow`'s CAS-based slot design.
followUps: Why is equality-check conflation important? (No spurious recompositions.)
How is this different from a plain `LiveData`? (Lifecycle-awareness is the LiveData add.)
What happens to a slow collector? (Conflation means it skips; a queue would buffer.)

items.q: Build a thread-safe in-memory key-value store
items.prompt:
Build a thread-safe `KeyValueStore` backed by a `HashMap`, with `get`/`put`/`remove`/`size`, used from multiple threads on Android.

Discuss the options in order: `synchronized` methods (correct, coarse), `ConcurrentHashMap` (fine-grained, but its `size()` and compound ops are not atomic), and per-key striping for hot paths. The interview is about *when* each is right and what compound operations (`getOrPut`) need.
hints: A plain `HashMap` is not thread-safe — concurrent puts can corrupt it or loop forever.
`ConcurrentHashMap` gives lock-free reads and per-bin locks. But `computeIfAbsent` is atomic while a read-then-write is not — say which.
For an 'image cache' style store, you often want an LRU policy too — mention `LinkedHashMap(accessOrder=true)` under a lock as the simple correct answer.

code.caption: ConcurrentHashMap with atomic compound ops

items.complexity: Time O(1) average for single-key ops (lock-free reads), O(bins) worst case. The eviction loop is not atomic — call it out; production LRU caches use `LruCache` for that reason.
followUps: Why is `map[key] = v; if (size > max) evict` not atomic? What races does it open?
When would a single `synchronized` map beat `ConcurrentHashMap`? (Very small stores, need atomic size+iterate.)
How would you add time-based expiry?

items.q: Exponential backoff with jitter for network retries
items.prompt:
Implement a retry helper that waits `initial * 2^attempt` before retrying, with full jitter — and explain why jitter matters.

The reason is thundering-herd prevention: without jitter, N clients all retry at the same synchronized instants, slamming the server. Full jitter (random between 0 and the backoff) breaks the synchronization. Know the three jitter styles (full, equal, decorrelated) well enough to discuss.
hints: Base backoff is `initialMs * 2^attempt`. Pure exponential still causes synchronized retry storms.
Full jitter: `Random.nextLong(0, backoff)`. Equal jitter: `backoff/2 ± Random.nextLong(0, backoff/2)`.
Cap the backoff (e.g. max 30s), and only retry on retryable errors (timeouts, 5xx), never on 4xx.

code.caption: Retry with capped full-jitter backoff

items.complexity: Time: at most maxAttempts calls with geometrically growing waits. The important output is the *policy*: retryable-error filter, cap, and jitter — not the loop itself.
followUps: Why is full jitter better than plain exponential for a fleet? (Thundering herd.)
Which errors should *not* be retried? (401, 400, SSL errors.)
How does this interact with OkHttp's built-in `RetryOnConnectionFailure`?

items.q: Build a bounded work queue with a worker pool
items.prompt:
Build a bounded work queue: producers submit tasks, a fixed pool of workers runs them, and when the queue is full the producer must back off (block, drop, or reject with a policy).

In Kotlin this is `Channel<T>(capacity)` + a pool of `launch`ed consumers — but the interview wants the *policy decisions*: what happens on full (blocking vs dropping vs throwing), how shutdown drains pending work, and how errors in one task don't kill the pool.
hints: `Channel(capacity, BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST / SUSPEND)` picks your overflow policy — say which you want and why.
A fixed pool: `repeat(workers) { scope.launch { for (job in channel) runCatching { job() } } }` — wrap each job so one failure doesn't stop the worker.
Shutdown: close the channel (producers stop), then `join` workers to drain. Distinguish 'drain then stop' from 'drop on shutdown'.

code.caption: Channel + fixed worker pool

items.complexity: Time O(1) submit when space, workers run concurrently; throughput bounded by workers. The buffer policy is the design point — SUSPEND gives natural backpressure, DROP_OLDEST suits stale work (e.g. images).
followUps: What's the difference between SUSPEND and DROP_OLDEST for a news-feed render queue?
How do you ensure a slow job doesn't starve the others? (No preemption in coroutines — fairness by design.)
What happens on process death — where's the durable variant?
